9
A ball falls vertically onto horizontal ground and rebounds, as shown.
p2
p1
before
after
The ball has momentum p1 downwards just before hitting the ground. After rebounding, the ball
leaves the ground with momentum p2 upwards. The ball is in contact with the ground for 0.020 s.
During this time interval, an average resultant force of 25 N acts on the ball.
What is a possible combination of values for p1 and p2?
p1 / kg m s–1
p2 / kg m s–1
A
0.15
0.65
B

0.15

hints: Notice $p_1$ is downwards before impact and $p_2$ is upwards after, so the total vector change is larger than either value alone.
Connect the 25 N average resultant force and 0.020 s contact time to change in momentum using $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$.
Calculate $F\Delta t$ in $\text{N s}$ and test which $p_1$, $p_2$ pair adds to that value with $p_1$ greater than $p_2$ for a losing bounce.
walkthrough: Take upwards as positive. Initial momentum is $-p_1$ and final momentum is $+p_2$, so change in momentum is $\Delta p = p_2 - (-p_1) = p_1 + p_2$.
Use impulse equals change in momentum: $\Delta p = F \Delta t$.
Substitute $F = 25 \text{ N}$ and $\Delta t = 0.020 \text{ s}$: $\Delta p = 25 \times 0.020 = 0.50 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.
Hence any possible pair must satisfy $p_1 + p_2 = 0.50 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.
For a real bounce some kinetic energy is lost, so expect $p_1 > p_2$. Only $p_1 = 0.30 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ and $p_2 = 0.20 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ satisfies both the sum and $p_1 > p_2$.

A.explanation: Sum $p_1 + p_2 = 0.80 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$, which gives impulse $0.80 \text{ N s}$, larger than the $0.50 \text{ N s}$ available.

B.explanation: Sum is $0.50 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ but $p_2 > p_1$, implying the rebound momentum is larger than the impact momentum, which is not physically possible for a normal bounce.

C.explanation: Sum $p_1 + p_2 = 0.50 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ matches $F\Delta t$, and $p_1 > p_2$ is consistent with some loss on rebound.

D.explanation: Sum $p_1 + p_2 = 0.80 \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$, which gives impulse $0.80 \text{ N s}$, larger than the $0.50 \text{ N s}$ available.
